query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Designing a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) microstructure with a fine, dual‐phase architecture – in which a ductile matrix contains finely dispersed, coherent precipitates arranged in a lamellar (e.g., δ‐lamellae with embedded γ″ particles) structure – will enable concurrent improvements in strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional HEA with a single-phase or coarse, homogeneous microstructure that exhibits either high strength with low ductility or vice versa.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermomechanical processing and aging treatment designed to generate a fine, coherent dual-phase (eutectic-like) microstructure with a ductile matrix and well-distributed second-phase precipitates.
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperature tensile loading conditions, where the microstructure can mediate plasticity.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent lamellar precipitates (δ-lamellae and embedded γ″ particles) within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates act as effective dislocation barriers (strengthening by precipitation hardening) while the lamellar architecture facilitates sequential dislocation cutting and shear reorientation, alleviating local stress concentrations and thereby enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed alloy will exhibit a higher yield strength while simultaneously showing improved uniform elongation and ductility compared to the single-phase or non-optimized microstructure.
generation.baseline: The mechanical properties (strength and ductility) of an HEA produced with conventional processing that results in a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.boundary: The method’s effectiveness may depend strongly on precise processing parameters and precipitate volume fraction; too high a fraction or loss of coherency may instead embrittle the alloy.
generation.uncertainty: Absolute improvements in strength and ductility are case specific. The quantitative benefits depend on alloy composition, processing conditions, and the final precipitate morphology. Further experimental validation is needed to delineate the processing window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set processed via the tailored thermomechanical plus aging treatment to create the fine, coherent lamellar dual-phase structure (experimental) and another set processed by conventional methods to yield a homogeneous microstructure (control). Conduct tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures.
measurements: TEM/SEM microstructural analysis to confirm precipitate size/distribution and coherency
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase structured (experimental) samples do not show statistically significant gains in both strength and ductility relative to the control samples, the hypothesis would be falsified.

Through TEM observations, we carefully characterized the evolution of the microstructure to discern the salient strengthening mechanisms generated by the SCCPs structure. Dislocation behavior at strains of 4%, 10%, and 14% in the W-based refractory HEA with the SCCPs structure are shown in Fig. 4 . Figure 4a–c, e reveal that dislocations cut through the δ-lamellae, yet are pinned by the γ ″ particles. For the coherent δ-lamellae structure, as the tensile stress increases up to the yield stress, dislocation slip occurs in the fcc matrix and involves shearing across the δ-lamellae, which indicates an early stage of the planar dislocation slip across the coherent δ/γ boundaries (Fig. 4a ). With further increase in strain to 10%, slip bands can clearly be observed across the δ-lamellae (Fig. 4b ). At a strain of 14%, shearing of the δ-lamellae by the slip bands leads to a large local shear (~40%) (Fig. 4c ), rather than the creation of a crack, which alleviates the local stress concentration. A schematic diagram of the interaction of dislocations with δ-lamellae is shown in Fig. 4d .

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
